This guide resolves the situation with practical criteria and avoids automatic fixes that can make the project worse or add unnecessary work.

The difference that matters

DMC's printed shade card reproduces colors on paper and is useful for locating codes and planning color families. DMC also sells a card with small real-thread swatches, which removes some uncertainty introduced by ink, paper and screens.

Before making a final decision, use a physical sample or reference whenever possible. Cross stitch repeats small differences across many stitches, so a tiny issue at the beginning can become very visible later. Material and construction

On its European site, DMC states that the current printed card lists 500 solid Mouliné Spécial colors plus additional thread ranges. It remains a useful organization tool even when a color-critical match is not required.

Record substitutions, materials and measurements. A simple note lets you repeat what worked and prevents the same question from needing to be researched halfway through the project. Applied to dmc color card: real thread vs printed chart, this check makes the decision more predictable before more time is invested.

Color, sheen and coverage

For choosing between two very close shades, the real-thread card is more reliable because sheen, texture and physical color can be viewed under the same light used for the actual skeins.

Judge the result in normal light and from normal viewing distance. A zoomed screen is useful for editing but does not reproduce the exact color, texture or reading of finished thread on fabric. Applied to dmc color card: real thread vs printed chart, this check makes the decision more predictable before more time is invested.

When substitution makes sense

The printed card is less costly and convenient for everyday reference. It can be enough for checking numbers, building an approximate palette or locating a color family quickly.

Avoid changing several variables at once. If fabric, thread and technique all change in one test, it becomes difficult to identify what caused an improvement or a problem. Applied to dmc color card: real thread vs printed chart, this check makes the decision more predictable before more time is invested.

When mixing is risky

For commercial pattern design, a real-thread card is particularly helpful with skin tones, gradients and substitutions. A stitched sample remains the final check because fabric changes how colors are perceived.

For valuable, antique or unknown materials, the prudent choice may be to stop. Not every problem needs a home treatment, and some interventions cannot be reversed. Applied to dmc color card: real thread vs printed chart, this check makes the decision more predictable before more time is invested.

How a pattern should state it

Do not treat screenshots of an online chart as a physical color reference. Displays, profiles and image compression prevent any guarantee that the shown shade matches the thread a customer will receive.

A quality PDF should anticipate the article's specific question with a short note, measurement or instruction.
